claim: The genus Cochlearia (Brassicaceae) originated from a drought-adapted Mediterranean sister genus during the Miocene.
source: Here, we reveal the enigmatic history of the genus Cochlearia (Brassicaceae), a Pleistocene relic that originated from a drought-adapted Mediterranean sister genus during the Miocene.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenomic analyses and divergence time estimates presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cochlearia rapidly diversified and adapted to circum-Arctic regions and other cold-characterized habitat types during the Pleistocene.
source: Cochlearia rapidly diversified and adapted to circum-Arctic regions and other cold-characterized habitat types during the Pleistocene.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data and divergence time estimates showing diversification during the Pleistocene.

claim: The sudden change in ecological preferences in Cochlearia was accompanied by a highly complex, reticulate polyploid evolution.
source: This sudden change in ecological preferences was accompanied by a highly complex, reticulate polyploid evolution, which was apparently triggered by the impact of repeated Pleistocene glaciation cycles.
evidence: This is supported by cytogenetic analyses and phylogenomic data showing polyploidy and reticulation.

claim: Repeated Pleistocene glaciation cycles triggered the complex, reticulate polyploid evolution in Cochlearia.
source: This sudden change in ecological preferences was accompanied by a highly complex, reticulate polyploid evolution, which was apparently triggered by the impact of repeated Pleistocene glaciation cycles.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal correlation between glaciation cycles and diversification events.

claim: Two early diversified Arctic-alpine diploid gene pools contributed differently to the evolution of the polyploid Cochlearia genus.
source: Our results illustrate that two early diversified Arctic-alpine diploid gene pools contributed differently to the evolution of this young polyploid genus now captured in a cold-adapted niche.
evidence: This is supported by nuclear genomic analyses and demographic modeling.

claim: Metabolomics revealed central carbon metabolism responses to cold in diverse Cochlearia species and ecotypes.
source: Metabolomics revealed central carbon metabolism responses to cold in diverse species and ecotypes, likely due to continuous connections to cold habitats that may have facilitated widespread adaptation to alpine and subalpine habitats, and which we speculate were coopted from existing drought adaptations.
evidence: This is supported by GC-MS metabolite profiling data.

claim: Cold adaptation in Cochlearia may have been coopted from existing drought adaptations.
source: Metabolomics revealed central carbon metabolism responses to cold in diverse species and ecotypes, likely due to continuous connections to cold habitats that may have facilitated widespread adaptation to alpine and subalpine habitats, and which we speculate were coopted from existing drought adaptations.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the shared osmotic stress mechanisms between drought and cold.

claim: Dynamic shifts in abiotic stressors lead to migration, adaptation, or extinction in organisms.
source: Dynamic shifts in these stressors lead to migration, adaptation, or extinction (Aitken et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Aitken et al., 2008.

claim: The current acceleration of global warming and climate volatility demands a better understanding of evolutionary dynamics resulting from climate change.
source: Thus, the current acceleration of global warming and climate volatility demands a better understanding of evolutionary dynamics resulting from climate change (Root et al., 2003; Thomas et al., 2004; Jump and Peñuelas, 2005; Visser, 2008; Franks et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: Plants typically lack the option of rapidly migrating away from changing conditions.
source: Further, there is a strong economic rationale for understanding the consequences of environmental change on plants, which typically lack the option of rapidly migrating away from changing conditions (Xoconostle-Cazares et al., 2010; Olsen and Wendel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about plant biology.

claim: Recurrent cycles of glaciation and deglaciation during the Pleistocene represent a powerful natural laboratory for the study of climate change adaptation.
source: An especially powerful natural laboratory for the study of climate change adaptation is represented by the recurrent cycles of glaciation and deglaciation during the Pleistocene.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The genus Cochlearia represents a promising study system for the evolutionary genomics of adaptation due to proximity to Arabidopsis and other Brassicaceae models.
source: The genus Cochlearia L. represents a promising study system for the evolutionary genomics of adaptation not only because of proximity to Arabidopsis and other Brassicaceae models, but also because of distinctive ecotypic traits which evolved within a short time span (Koch et al., 1996; Koch et al., 1998; Koch et al., 1999; Koch, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on Cochlearia.

claim: Cochlearia has distinctive ecotypic traits which evolved within a short time span.
source: The genus Cochlearia L. represents a promising study system for the evolutionary genomics of adaptation not only because of proximity to Arabidopsis and other Brassicaceae models, but also because of distinctive ecotypic traits which evolved within a short time span (Koch et al., 1996; Koch et al., 1998; Koch et al., 1999; Koch, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cochlearia has adaptations to extreme bedrock types (dolomite versus siliceous).
source: Among these are adaptations to extreme bedrock types (dolomite versus siliceous), heavy metal-rich soils, diverse salt habitats, high alpine regions, and life cycle variation.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the genus based on established knowledge.

claim: Cochlearia has adaptations to heavy metal-rich soils.
source: Among these are adaptations to extreme bedrock types (dolomite versus siliceous), heavy metal-rich soils, diverse salt habitats, high alpine regions, and life cycle variation.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the genus based on established knowledge.

claim: Cochlearia has adaptations to diverse salt habitats.
source: Among these are adaptations to extreme bedrock types (dolomite versus siliceous), heavy metal-rich soils, diverse salt habitats, high alpine regions, and life cycle variation.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the genus based on established knowledge.

claim: Cochlearia has adaptations to high alpine regions.
source: Among these are adaptations to extreme bedrock types (dolomite versus siliceous), heavy metal-rich soils, diverse salt habitats, high alpine regions, and life cycle variation.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the genus based on established knowledge.

claim: Cochlearia exhibits life cycle variation.
source: Among these are adaptations to extreme bedrock types (dolomite versus siliceous), heavy metal-rich soils, diverse salt habitats, high alpine regions, and life cycle variation.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the genus based on established knowledge.

claim: Cochlearia has a remarkably dynamic cytogenetic evolution.
source: This diversity is accompanied by a remarkably dynamic cytogenetic evolution within the genus.
evidence: This is supported by cytogenetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two base chromosome numbers exist in Cochlearia (n=6 and n=7).
source: Two base chromosome numbers exist (n=6 and n=7) and out of the 20 accepted taxa, two-thirds are neopolyploids, ranging from tetraploids to octoploids (previous phylogenetic hypotheses are given in Appendix 1—figure 1; see Supplementary file 1 and Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is supported by cytogenetic data.

claim: Out of the 20 accepted Cochlearia taxa, two-thirds are neopolyploids, ranging from tetraploids to octoploids.
source: Two base chromosome numbers exist (n=6 and n=7) and out of the 20 accepted taxa, two-thirds are neopolyploids, ranging from tetraploids to octoploids (previous phylogenetic hypotheses are given in Appendix 1—figure 1; see Supplementary file 1 and Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is supported by cytogenetic data and literature review.

claim: The cold character of diverse habitat types in Cochlearia stands in sharp contrast to the preferences of the sole outgroup sister genus Ionopsidium, which occurs only in arid Mediterranean habitats.
source: The connecting element between the various cytotypes and ecotypes is the cold character of the diverse habitat types standing in sharp contrast to the preferences of the sole outgroup sister genus Ionopsidium, which occurs only in arid Mediterranean habitats (Koch, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koch, 2012.

claim: Cochlearia and Ionopsidium constitute the monophyletic tribe Cochlearieae with a stem group age of approximately 18.9 million years ago.
source: These two genera constitute the monophyletic tribe Cochlearieae with a stem group age of approx. 18.9 million years ago (Walden et al., 2020) and which forms with various other tribes from Brassicaceae the rapidly emerging evolutionary lineage II with highest net diversification rates 16–23 million years ago (Walden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Walden et al., 2020.

claim: The tribe Cochlearieae forms with various other tribes from Brassicaceae the rapidly emerging evolutionary lineage II with highest net diversification rates 16–23 million years ago.
source: These two genera constitute the monophyletic tribe Cochlearieae with a stem group age of approx. 18.9 million years ago (Walden et al., 2020) and which forms with various other tribes from Brassicaceae the rapidly emerging evolutionary lineage II with highest net diversification rates 16–23 million years ago (Walden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Walden et al., 2020.

claim: The genus Cochlearia comprises 16 accepted species and 4 subspecies.
source: In total, the genus Cochlearia comprises 16 accepted species and 4 subspecies (Kiefer et al., 2014, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kiefer et al., 2014.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, drought- and temperature-adaptive genetic variants are shared among Mediterranean and Nordic regions.
source: While on species-level it has been shown in Arabidopsis thaliana that drought- and temperature-adaptive genetic variants are shared among Mediterranean and Nordic regions (Exposito-Alonso et al., 2017), the separation of Cochlearia from Ionopsidium is much deeper, dating to the mid-Miocene (Koch, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Exposito-Alonso et al., 2017.

claim: The separation of Cochlearia from Ionopsidium dates to the mid-Miocene.
source: While on species-level it has been shown in Arabidopsis thaliana that drought- and temperature-adaptive genetic variants are shared among Mediterranean and Nordic regions (Exposito-Alonso et al., 2017), the separation of Cochlearia from Ionopsidium is much deeper, dating to the mid-Miocene (Koch, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koch, 2012.

claim: The formation of the genus Cochlearia as we see it today first started during the middle (0.77–0.13 mya) and late (0.13–0.012 mya) Pleistocene.
source: However, the formation of the genus Cochlearia as we see it today first started much more recently, during the middle (0.77–0.13 mya) and late (0.13–0.012 mya) Pleistocene (Koch, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koch, 2012.

claim: There is a long lag between the divergence of Ionopsidium and Cochlearia, raising the hypothesis of a long-lasting footprint of drought adaptation in Cochlearia.
source: This long lag between the divergence of the sole outgroup Ionopsidium and Cochlearia raises the hypothesis of a long-lasting footprint of drought adaptation in Cochlearia.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from phylogenetic data.

claim: The strong association with cold habitats shown by almost all Cochlearia species may be interpreted as a cold preference that was acquired rapidly in adaptation to the intense climatic fluctuations which characterized the Pleistocene epoch.
source: The strong association with cold habitats shown by almost all Cochlearia species may therefore be interpreted as a cold preference that was acquired rapidly in adaptation to the intense climatic fluctuations which characterized this epoch.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on phylogenetic and ecological data.

claim: There is a growing interest in the genus Cochlearia from diverse fields.
source: There is a growing interest in the genus Cochlearia from diverse fields (Reeves, 2019; Brock et al., 2006; Dauvergne et al., 2006; Brandrud et al., 2017; Mandáková et al., 2017; Nawaz et al., 2017; Bray et al., 2020), but the evolutionary history of the genus has been highly recalcitrant.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The evolutionary history of the genus Cochlearia has been highly recalcitrant.
source: There is a growing interest in the genus Cochlearia from diverse fields (Reeves, 2019; Brock et al., 2006; Dauvergne et al., 2006; Brandrud et al., 2017; Mandáková et al., 2017; Nawaz et al., 2017; Bray et al., 2020), but the evolutionary history of the genus has been highly recalcitrant.
evidence: This is a statement about the difficulty of resolving Cochlearia phylogeny.

claim: It is still unknown how Cochlearia managed the rapid transition from Mediterranean to circum-Arctic or high-alpine habitat types in combination with a highly dynamic cytogenetic evolution.
source: Thus it is still unknown how the genus managed the rapid transition from Mediterranean to circum-Arctic or high-alpine habitat types in combination with a highly dynamic cytogenetic evolution.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: The cold metabolome in A. thaliana can reflect continental-scale biogeographically defined clines along temperature gradients.
source: However, since it has been shown for A. thaliana that the cold metabolome can reflect continental-scale biogeographically defined clines along temperature gradients (Pritchard et al., 2000; Weiszmann et al., 2020), it can be assumed that on evolutionary scales past footprints of diversification might be detectable, and that in principle genomic analyses (e.g., GWAS) may allow to identify candidate genes involved in pathway regulation and metabolic reaction plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pritchard et al., 2000 and Weiszmann et al., 2020.

claim: On evolutionary scales, past footprints of diversification might be detectable in the metabolome.
source: However, since it has been shown for A. thaliana that the cold metabolome can reflect continental-scale biogeographically defined clines along temperature gradients (Pritchard et al., 2000; Weiszmann et al., 2020), it can be assumed that on evolutionary scales past footprints of diversification might be detectable, and that in principle genomic analyses (e.g., GWAS) may allow to identify candidate genes involved in pathway regulation and metabolic reaction plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from A. thaliana studies.

claim: Genomic analyses (e.g., GWAS) may allow identification of candidate genes involved in pathway regulation and metabolic reaction plasticity.
source: However, since it has been shown for A. thaliana that the cold metabolome can reflect continental-scale biogeographically defined clines along temperature gradients (Pritchard et al., 2000; Weiszmann et al., 2020), it can be assumed that on evolutionary scales past footprints of diversification might be detectable, and that in principle genomic analyses (e.g., GWAS) may allow to identify candidate genes involved in pathway regulation and metabolic reaction plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future analyses.

claim: The phylogenetic and cytogenetic analysis uncovers a recurrent boosting of speciation by glaciation cycles in Cochlearia.
source: Our phylogenetic and cytogenetic analysis uncovers a recurrent boosting of speciation by glaciation cycles in this cytotypically very diverse genus and indicates that, despite clear challenges brought by global warming, the genus survives evolutionarily while, we speculate, rescuing its species diversity with reticulate and polyploid evolution.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic and cytogenetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Despite clear challenges brought by global warming, the genus Cochlearia survives evolutionarily while rescuing its species diversity with reticulate and polyploid evolution.
source: Our phylogenetic and cytogenetic analysis uncovers a recurrent boosting of speciation by glaciation cycles in this cytotypically very diverse genus and indicates that, despite clear challenges brought by global warming, the genus survives evolutionarily while, we speculate, rescuing its species diversity with reticulate and polyploid evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed patterns of reticulation and polyploidy.

claim: A comprehensive survey of 575 georeferenced chromosome counts and/or genome sizes across the Cochlearia genus was generated.
source: In order to first resolve its cytogenetic evolution, we generated a comprehensive survey of 575 georeferenced chromosome counts and/or genome sizes across the Cochlearia genus (Supplementary file 2) based on our novel cytogenetic data (Supplementary file 3) and a review of published literature over the last century (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in supplementary files.

claim: There is a clear continental-scale geographical partitioning of diploid cytotypes (2n=12 and 2n=14) in Cochlearia.
source: This survey revealed a clear continental-scale geographical partitioning of diploid cytotypes (2n=12 and 2n=14; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Highly dynamic genome compositions are observed throughout the Cochlearia genus, with widespread aneuploidies and DNA content variation.
source: We observed highly dynamic genome compositions throughout the genus, with widespread aneuploidies (aberrations from typical species-specific chromosome numbers) and DNA content variation.
evidence: This is supported by cytogenetic data.

claim: Aneuploidies are frequently found in polyploid Cochlearia taxa, especially along the coasts.
source: Aneuploidies are frequently found in polyploid Cochlearia taxa, especially along the coasts (Figure 1b), but they are only rarely spotted in diploids and therefore are nearly absent from Arctic regions, where only diploids are observed (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1b and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Aneuploidies are only rarely spotted in diploid Cochlearia and are nearly absent from Arctic regions, where only diploids are observed.
source: Aneuploidies are frequently found in polyploid Cochlearia taxa, especially along the coasts (Figure 1b), but they are only rarely spotted in diploids and therefore are nearly absent from Arctic regions, where only diploids are observed (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1b and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The high frequency of polyploidization events in Cochlearia is accompanied by increasing genome sizes.
source: Both analyses revealed that (1) the high frequency of polyploidization events is accompanied by increasing genome sizes (Appendix 1—figure 4), while there is (2) a slight but significant negative correlation of chromosome size with increasing chromosome numbers (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses and data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: There is a slight but significant negative correlation of chromosome size with increasing chromosome numbers in Cochlearia.
source: Both analyses revealed that (1) the high frequency of polyploidization events is accompanied by increasing genome sizes (Appendix 1—figure 4), while there is (2) a slight but significant negative correlation of chromosome size with increasing chromosome numbers (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses and data shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: The trend of chromosome size reduction with increasing chromosome numbers was independent of inclusion or exclusion of the annual species C. danica and the short-lived Arctic diploids.
source: This trend was independent of inclusion or exclusion of the annual species C. danica and the short-lived Arctic diploids.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses.

claim: A relationship between lower genome size and annuality was shown as a significant trend for the Brassicaceae as a whole.
source: These taxa were treated as putative outliers because a relationship between lower genome size and annuality was shown as a significant trend for the Brassicaceae as a whole (Hohmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hohmann et al., 2015.

claim: Extensive past hybridization and reticulate evolution of polyploid taxa results in complex evolutionary scenarios in Cochlearia.
source: Extensive past hybridization and reticulate evolution of polyploid taxa results in complex evolutionary scenarios, which are often not well resolved by strict phylogenetic reconstruction using nuclear data.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of phylogenetic reconstruction in Cochlearia.

claim: Genome sequence data for 65 Cochlearia accessions, representing all accepted Cochlearia species, as well as three species from the sister genus Ionopsidium were generated.
source: To provide a highly resolved organellar phylogeny, we generated genome sequence data for 65 Cochlearia accessions, representing all accepted Cochlearia species, as well as three species from the sister genus Ionopsidium (Appendix 1—figure 5 and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This describes the data generation for the study.

claim: Complete plastid genomes were assembled de novo for all 65 Cochlearia and 3 Ionopsidium samples.
source: Using these data, complete plastid genomes were assembled de novo for all samples.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods.

claim: A maximum likelihood analysis based on whole chloroplast genome alignment revealed six well-supported major lineages within the genus Cochlearia.
source: A maximum likelihood (ML) analysis using RAxML based on our whole chloroplast genome alignment (122,798 bp, excluding one copy of the inverted repeat) covering a total of 5292 SNPs (1003 within Cochlearia) revealed six well-supported major lineages within the genus (Appendix 1—figure 6, congruent to lineages as illustrated in BEAST chronogram, Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 6 and Figure 2.

claim: A radiation of plastome diversity in Cochlearia was indicated by the existence of several polytomies.
source: A radiation of plastome diversity was indicated by the existence of several polytomies, despite the generally high resolution of the ML tree.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic tree topology.

claim: The plastid and mitochondrial phylogenies of Cochlearia are largely consistent.
source: The two maternal phylogenies are largely consistent, and after collapsing all branches below a bootstrap support of 95%, no incongruences remained (illustrated by a tanglegram in Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the tanglegram shown in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: Divergence time estimates based on plastid genome data revealed diversification bursts that closely coincide with high glacial periods.
source: Divergence time estimates generated with BEAST based on our whole plastid genome alignment revealed diversification bursts that closely coincide with high glacial periods.
evidence: This is supported by the BEAST analysis and divergence time estimates.

claim: The BEAST analysis shows a diversification of the entire Cochlearia genus within the last ~660 kya.
source: In accordance with Hohmann et al., 2015, our BEAST analysis shows a diversification of the entire genus within the last ~660 kya, after a long period of evolutionary stasis and zero net diversification following a deep split from the genus Ionopsidium ~9.25 mya (see also Koch, 2012), and in concert with the beginning of the Pleistocene's major climatic fluctuations, which are dated to 700 kya (Webb and Bartlein, 1992; Comes and Kadereit, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the BEAST analysis and citations.

claim: There was a long period of evolutionary stasis and zero net diversification in Cochlearia following a deep split from the genus Ionopsidium ~9.25 mya.
source: In accordance with Hohmann et al., 2015, our BEAST analysis shows a diversification of the entire genus within the last ~660 kya, after a long period of evolutionary stasis and zero net diversification following a deep split from the genus Ionopsidium ~9.25 mya (see also Koch, 2012), and in concert with the beginning of the Pleistocene's major climatic fluctuations, which are dated to 700 kya (Webb and Bartlein, 1992; Comes and Kadereit, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the BEAST analysis and citations.

claim: The diversification of Cochlearia occurred in concert with the beginning of the Pleistocene's major climatic fluctuations, which are dated to 700 kya.
source: In accordance with Hohmann et al., 2015, our BEAST analysis shows a diversification of the entire genus within the last ~660 kya, after a long period of evolutionary stasis and zero net diversification following a deep split from the genus Ionopsidium ~9.25 mya (see also Koch, 2012), and in concert with the beginning of the Pleistocene's major climatic fluctuations, which are dated to 700 kya (Webb and Bartlein, 1992; Comes and Kadereit, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the BEAST analysis and citations to Webb and Bartlein, 1992 and Comes and Kadereit, 1998.

claim: Diversification times in the six major chloroplast lineages of Cochlearia closely coincide with high glacial periods.
source: Thus, diversification times in the six major chloroplast lineages as revealed via both ML and BEAST analysis closely coincide with high glacial periods (Petit et al., 1999; see timeline in Figure 2; Augustin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses and timeline shown in Figure 2.

claim: The most basal Cochlearia chloroplast and mitochondrial haplotypes were found in Eastern Canadian C. tridactylites.
source: The most basal Cochlearia chloroplast and mitochondrial haplotypes (yellow lineage – Arctic I) were found in Eastern Canadian C. tridactylites, a species of unknown ploidy (Appendix 2), in a region where ice-free areas putatively occurred during the Penultimate Glacial Period (~140 kya; Colleoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses and a citation to Colleoni et al., 2016.

claim: Ice-free areas putatively occurred in Eastern Canada during the Penultimate Glacial Period (~140 kya).
source: The most basal Cochlearia chloroplast and mitochondrial haplotypes (yellow lineage – Arctic I) were found in Eastern Canadian C. tridactylites, a species of unknown ploidy (Appendix 2), in a region where ice-free areas putatively occurred during the Penultimate Glacial Period (~140 kya; Colleoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Colleoni et al., 2016.

claim: The earliest diverged organellar genomes of known diploids in Cochlearia were found in the Arctic species C. groenlandica and C. sessilifolia.
source: The earliest diverged organellar genomes of known diploids were found in the Arctic species C. groenlandica and C. sessilifolia (collected in British Columbia, Canada, and Kodiak Island, Alaska, respectively; pink lineage (Arctic II) in Figure 2, see Appendix 1—figure 6 for details), with distribution ranges covering areas such as Beringia that were thought to have served as ice-free Pleistocene refugia (Abbott and Brochmann, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2 and Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Beringia was thought to have served as ice-free Pleistocene refugia.
source: The earliest diverged organellar genomes of known diploids were found in the Arctic species C. groenlandica and C. sessilifolia (collected in British Columbia, Canada, and Kodiak Island, Alaska, respectively; pink lineage (Arctic II) in Figure 2, see Appendix 1—figure 6 for details), with distribution ranges covering areas such as Beringia that were thought to have served as ice-free Pleistocene refugia (Abbott and Brochmann, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Abbott and Brochmann, 2003.

claim: European diploids in Cochlearia are found in the green (Arctic-European) and purple (western European) lineages only.
source: European diploids are found in the green (Arctic-European) and purple (western European) lineages only.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Some European polyploids harbor early diverged haplotypes from the otherwise pink (Arctic II) lineage.
source: Some of the European polyploids, however, harbor early diverged haplotypes from the otherwise pink (Arctic II) lineage.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Except for the eastern European C. borzaeana with 2n=8x=48, all taxa from the pink lineage, as well as several taxa from the early diverged blue and orange lineages, have a base chromosome number of n=7.
source: Thus, except for the eastern European C. borzaeana with 2n=8x=48, all taxa from the pink lineage, as well as several taxa from the early diverged blue (Coastal Western European) and orange (Eastern European) lineages, have a base chromosome number of n=7 (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by cytogenetic data and phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2.

claim: A phylogenetic network using SplitsTree based on 447,919 biallelic SNPs shows a clear separation of Arctic and European diploid taxa.
source: For 63 samples with sufficient nuclear sequence data quality (62 Cochlearia samples and Ionopsidium megalospermum), we generated a phylogenetic network using SplitsTree (Huson, 1998; Huson and Bryant, 2006) based on 447,919 biallelic SNPs. Concordant with our cytogenetic results, the network shows a clear separation of Arctic and European diploid taxa (Figure 3a and b; see Appendix 1—figure 11 for detailed SplitsTree output).
evidence: This is supported by the SplitsTree analysis shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: Close associations of both C. tridactylites and C. danica with Ionopsidium support the picture as revealed from organellar phylogenies.
source: Close associations of both C. tridactylites and C. danica with Ionopsidium support the picture as revealed from organellar phylogenies.
evidence: This is supported by the SplitsTree and ML analyses.

claim: An ML analysis based on 298,978 variant sites provides further support for the early divergence of C. tridactylites and C. danica.
source: Further support for the early divergence of these two species came from an ML analysis based on 298,978 variant sites (same set of samples) performed with RAxML using an ascertainment bias correction and a general time-reversible substitution model assuming gamma distribution (Appendix 1—figure 12).
evidence: This is supported by the ML analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 12.

claim: Organellar and nuclear phylogenies are not congruent for single polyploid taxa in Cochlearia.
source: Referring to single polyploid taxa, organellar and nuclear phylogenies are not congruent (Appendix 1—figure 6 and Appendix 1—figure 12), which is best explained by the often allopolyploid origin of the tetraploids (e.g., C. bavarica, Appendix 1—figure 13 and Appendix 1—figure 14), which may be even complicated by multiple and polytopic origin and further reticulation.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of phylogenies shown in Appendix 1—figure 6 and Appendix 1—figure 12.

claim: The incongruence between organellar and nuclear phylogenies for polyploid taxa is best explained by the often allopolyploid origin of the tetraploids.
source: Referring to single polyploid taxa, organellar and nuclear phylogenies are not congruent (Appendix 1—figure 6 and Appendix 1—figure 12), which is best explained by the often allopolyploid origin of the tetraploids (e.g., C. bavarica, Appendix 1—figure 13 and Appendix 1—figure 14), which may be even complicated by multiple and polytopic origin and further reticulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic data.

claim: A STRUCTURE analysis of Cochlearia samples with K=3 revealed a pattern very similar to that obtained via SplitsTree, showing the two diploid clusters and a third cluster comprising C. danica samples.
source: A STRUCTURE analysis of Cochlearia samples only (same variant calling, 400,071 variants after excluding Ionopsidium) with K=3 (optimal K following Evanno Method; Evanno et al., 2005) revealed a pattern very similar to that obtained via SplitsTree, showing the two diploid clusters and a third cluster comprising C. danica samples (Figure 3b and Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: This is supported by the STRUCTURE analysis shown in Figure 3b and Appendix 1—figure 15.

claim: There are potential signatures of admixture between the diploid clusters in Cochlearia, especially in Icelandic 2n=12 and 2n=14 diploids and in several polyploid samples such as C. bavarica.
source: We note potential signatures of admixture between the diploid clusters, especially in Icelandic 2n=12 and 2n=14 diploids and in several polyploid samples such as C. bavarica (discussed in detail in Appendix 1).
evidence: This is supported by the STRUCTURE analysis.

claim: C. tridactylites was modeled as a mix of the Arctic gene pool and C. danica in the STRUCTURE analysis.
source: Interestingly, C. tridactylites, the earliest diverged lineage according to the plastome analysis, was modeled as a mix of the Arctic gene pool and C. danica.
evidence: This is supported by the STRUCTURE analysis.

claim: In a TreeMix analysis, C. tridactylites is admixed, with a majority ancestry from near the base of the European and Arctic groups, and a minority ancestry from the 2n=14 group of Arctic diploids.
source: In a separate TreeMix (Pickrell and Pritchard, 2012) analysis of all Cochlearia accessions and Ionopsidium (447,919 variants; up to 10 migration events), the bootstrapped graph for m=1 (optimal number of migration events according to Evanno Method; Appendix 1—figure 16) likewise indicates that C. tridactylites is admixed, with a majority ancestry from near the base of the European (excepting hexaploid C. danica) and Arctic groups, and a minority ancestry from the 2n=14 group of Arctic diploids (see Appendix 1—figures 17–19).
evidence: This is supported by the TreeMix analysis shown in Appendix 1—figures 16-19.

claim: The EUR metapopulation exhibits much higher genetic diversity than the ARC metapopulation.
source: Overall, the EUR metapopulation exhibits much higher genetic diversity than the ARC metapopulation (Supplementary file 8), which is in accordance with population-based analyses (Koch et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by genetic diversity statistics in Supplementary file 8 and a citation to Koch et al., 1998.

claim: In both EUR and ARC populations, there is an excess of rare alleles (negative Tajima's D), indicating that they are not in mutation-drift equilibrium.
source: In both populations, 2n=12 and 2n=14, we found an excess of rare alleles (negative Tajima's D, Supplementary file 8), indicating that they are not in mutation-drift equilibrium.
evidence: This is supported by Tajima's D statistics in Supplementary file 8.

claim: Differentiation and divergence between ARC and EUR were overall very low (Fst ~0.098, dxy ~0.0036).
source: Differentiation and divergence between ARC and EUR were overall very low (Fst ~0.098, dxy ~0.0036, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by population genetic statistics in Supplementary file 8.

claim: After the EUR and ARC metapopulations separated, they underwent dramatic changes in effective population sizes (Ne) over time.
source: Given the dynamic nature of their ice-age-associated speciation histories, we hypothesized that after the EUR and ARC metapopulations separated, they underwent dramatic changes in effective population sizes (Ne) over time, and that they experienced gene flow.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by ABC modeling.

claim: Discriminating between the four gene flow models (SI, CM, OSC, PSC) was ambiguous in the ABC analysis.
source: However, discriminating between the four gene flow models was ambiguous (see Supplementary file 9), as the most probable model depended on the priors, particularly on the upper bound of the Ne priors.
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results in Supplementary file 9.

claim: When allowing Ne up to 400,000, a model of ongoing secondary contact (OSC) prevailed over a model without any gene flow (model SI).
source: When allowing Ne up to 400,000, a model of ongoing secondary contact (OSC) prevailed over a model without any gene flow (model SI; posterior probability >0.75, i.e., Bayes Factor >3), but OSC was not clearly better than a model with continuous gene flow (CM) or a past secondary contact (PSC).
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results.

claim: When choosing a less informative Ne prior with a greater upper bound of three million, all four gene flow models were similarly in agreement with the observed data.
source: Yet, when choosing a less informative Ne prior with a greater upper bound of three million, all four models were similarly in agreement with the observed data.
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results.

claim: In the absence of strong prior information for Ne, the occurrence of gene flow between ARC and EUR metapopulations could not be established with confidence.
source: In the absence of strong prior information for Ne, we could not establish the occurrence of gene flow between ARC and EUR metapopulations with confidence (see Appendix 3 for further information on ABC model choice).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ABC modeling results.

claim: The model without gene flow (SI) with a smaller Ne prior bound of maximal 400,000 provided the best fit to the data.
source: The model without gene flow (SI) contained the fewest parameters, and this model with a smaller Ne prior bound of maximal 400,000 provided the best fit to the data (smallest Euclidean distances between observed and predicted values from posterior predictive checks; see Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results in Supplementary file 11.

claim: All ABC model fits agreed that the EUR metapopulation had risen to 4–12-fold the Ne of their common ancestral population followed by a moderate decline or constant size up to the present.
source: Importantly, all model fits agreed about the relative Ne of EUR and ARC: they evolved drastically differently, with the EUR metapopulation having risen to 4–12-fold the Ne of their common ancestral population followed by a moderate decline (0.4–0.8-fold in three out of four models), or constant size up to the present (OSC with smaller Ne upper bound).
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results.

claim: The ARC metapopulation experienced a bottleneck after splitting from the common ancestor (0.2–0.5-fold), followed by a dramatic expansion of 9–52-fold.
source: In contrast, the ARC metapopulation experienced a bottleneck after splitting from the common ancestor (0.2–0.5-fold), followed by a dramatic expansion of 9–52-fold (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results in Supplementary file 10.

claim: If EUR and ARC did not experience gene flow (SI model fit), they must have separated only about 65,000–73,000 generations ago.
source: If EUR and ARC did not experience gene flow (SI model fit), they must have separated only about 65,000–73,000 generations ago, corresponding to 0.2–3 Ne units.
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results.

claim: The split time estimate of 65,000–73,000 generations ago may coincide with the last interglacial period (considering a 2-year average generation time).
source: This estimate was robust to the choice of priors and may coincide with the last interglacial period (considering a 2-year average generation time; Abs, 1999).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ABC modeling results and a citation to Abs, 1999.

claim: If gene flow is assumed (OSC), the split between EUR and ARC could have occurred earlier (119,000–227,000 generations ago).
source: If gene flow is assumed (OSC), this split could have occurred earlier (119,000–227,000 generations ago; Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results in Supplementary file 10.

claim: Polyploid inland taxa, such as alpine hexaploid C. tatrae from the High Tatra mountains, showing footprints of both diploid gene pools cannot have evolved earlier than during the Last Interglacial.
source: Considering our BEAST analyses from plastome data, a split-time of 65,000–73,000 generations ago is more likely (e.g., dating of splits within the green evolutionary lineage). An important implication of this is that polyploid inland taxa, such as alpine hexaploid C. tatrae from the High Tatra mountains, showing footprints of both diploid gene pools cannot have evolved earlier than during the Last Interglacial.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ABC modeling and BEAST analyses.

claim: Hexaploid C. bavarica showed a postglacial origin and footprint of both diploid gene pools dated with approximately 12–15,000 years ago predating rapid Holocenic temperature increase.
source: The example of hexaploid C. bavarica showed a postglacial origin and footprint of both diploid gene pools dated with approximately 12–15,000 years ago predating rapid Holocenic temperature increase.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and demographic analyses.

claim: A very early evolved tolerance to cold facilitated the observed widespread adaptation to alpine and subalpine habitats across the Cochlearia genus.
source: We hypothesized that a very early evolved tolerance to cold facilitated the observed widespread adaptation to alpine and subalpine habitats across the Cochlearia genus.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by metabolite profiling.

claim: Metabolite profiling of central carbon metabolism using GC-MS was performed for 28 worldwide Cochlearia accessions, including 14 taxa and 5 outgroup accessions (genus Ionopsidium).
source: To test this hypothesis, we performed metabolite profiling of central carbon metabolism using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) for 28 worldwide Cochlearia accessions, including 14 taxa and 5 outgroup accessions (genus Ionopsidium; sampling details in Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Principal component analysis based on 19 WorldClim temperature and precipitation-based bioclimatic variables distribute 46.8%, 29.6%, and 12.4% of variance with components 1, 2, and 3, respectively.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) based on 19 WorldClim temperature and precipitation-based bioclimatic variables distribute 46.8%, 29.6%, and 12.4% of variance with components 1, 2, and 3, respectively (Appendix 1—figure 20).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA results shown in Appendix 1—figure 20.

claim: A KMO test showed significant difference between the correlation matrix of variables and an identity matrix (KMO=0.53, df 171, p<0.001) for the 19 bioclimatic variables.
source: A KMO test showed significant difference between the correlation matrix of variables and an identity matrix (KMO=0.53, df 171, p<0.001; Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical test results in Supplementary file 12.

claim: Four major bioclimatically defined clusters were recognized in Cochlearia based on hierarchical cluster analysis of nine WorldClim bioclimatic variables.
source: For the Cochlearia accessions, we found the same four bioclimatically defined clusters based on a hierarchical cluster analysis of nine WorldClim bioclimatic variables chosen as most important for species' growth and fitness according to our field and cultivation experiences (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the hierarchical cluster analysis shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: Cluster 1 combines coastal polyploid accessions from the northern UK.
source: Cluster 1 combines coastal polyploid accessions from the northern UK; Cluster 2 includes European inland accessions (diploids and polyploids); Cluster 3 comprises European accessions with Arctic/alpine habitat types (Norway, Carpathians, High Tatra Mountains, and Austrian Alps); and cluster four includes Arctic accessions (Iceland, Alaska) and those from alpine habitat types from the UK.
evidence: This describes the composition of the bioclimatic clusters.

claim: Cluster 2 includes European inland accessions (diploids and polyploids).
source: Cluster 1 combines coastal polyploid accessions from the northern UK; Cluster 2 includes European inland accessions (diploids and polyploids); Cluster 3 comprises European accessions with Arctic/alpine habitat types (Norway, Carpathians, High Tatra Mountains, and Austrian Alps); and cluster four includes Arctic accessions (Iceland, Alaska) and those from alpine habitat types from the UK.
evidence: This describes the composition of the bioclimatic clusters.

claim: Cluster 3 comprises European accessions with Arctic/alpine habitat types (Norway, Carpathians, High Tatra Mountains, and Austrian Alps).
source: Cluster 1 combines coastal polyploid accessions from the northern UK; Cluster 2 includes European inland accessions (diploids and polyploids); Cluster 3 comprises European accessions with Arctic/alpine habitat types (Norway, Carpathians, High Tatra Mountains, and Austrian Alps); and cluster four includes Arctic accessions (Iceland, Alaska) and those from alpine habitat types from the UK.
evidence: This describes the composition of the bioclimatic clusters.

claim: Cluster 4 includes Arctic accessions (Iceland, Alaska) and those from alpine habitat types from the UK.
source: Cluster 1 combines coastal polyploid accessions from the northern UK; Cluster 2 includes European inland accessions (diploids and polyploids); Cluster 3 comprises European accessions with Arctic/alpine habitat types (Norway, Carpathians, High Tatra Mountains, and Austrian Alps); and cluster four includes Arctic accessions (Iceland, Alaska) and those from alpine habitat types from the UK.
evidence: This describes the composition of the bioclimatic clusters.

claim: Ionopsidium represented a fifth, Mediterranean, bioclimatically defined group.
source: Ionopsidium represented a fifth, Mediterranean, bioclimatically defined group.
evidence: This describes the bioclimatic classification of Ionopsidium.

claim: Metabolic profiles were collected before and after a 20-day treatment under cold (5°C) or control conditions (18°C/20°C).
source: For all groups, metabolic profiles were collected before and after a 20-day treatment under cold (5°C) or control conditions (18°C/20°C; Figure 4c).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Peak areas for a set of 40 compounds consistently detected across samples were exported, annotated as intermediates within central carbon metabolic pathways.
source: From these profiles, we exported peak areas for a set of 40 compounds consistently detected across our samples that were annotated as intermediates within central carbon metabolic pathways (see Supplementary file 13 for a list of detected compounds; raw/normalized data provided in Supplementary file 14).
evidence: This describes the metabolite data extraction.

claim: Increases in the relative levels of many of the targeted compounds were generally found after the cold treatment, especially for carbohydrates and amino acids.
source: As has been best seen in the Arabidopsis cold stress metabolome (Cook et al., 2004; Kaplan et al., 2004; Kaplan et al., 2007), we generally found increases in the relative levels of many of the targeted compounds after the cold treatment, especially for carbohydrates and amino acids, exemplifying a similar physiological mechanism (data grouped by bioclimatic clusters, analyzed by one-way ANOVAs; Appendix 1—figures 22–27).
evidence: This is supported by the metabolite data and citations to Arabidopsis studies.

claim: Significant increases in carbohydrate levels as a well-known reaction to cold stress in plants were detected in all analyzed carbohydrates except for sucrose.
source: Significant increases in carbohydrate levels as a well-known reaction to cold stress in plants were detected in all herein analyzed carbohydrates except for sucrose.
evidence: This is supported by the metabolite data.

claim: Important functions of various carbohydrates as cryoprotectants and/or signaling molecules in the plant cold response have been suggested before, for glucose and mannose.
source: Important functions of various carbohydrates as cryoprotectants and/or signaling molecules in the plant cold response have been suggested before, for glucose (reviewed by Janská et al., 2010) and mannose (Davey et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janská et al., 2010 and Davey et al., 2008.

claim: Proline is well known for its role in the plant response to various abiotic stresses including low temperatures.
source: Among the analyzed amino acids showing increased levels after cold treatment, proline is well known for its role in the plant response to various abiotic stresses including low temperatures (e.g., reviewed by Ashraf and Foolad, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ashraf and Foolad, 2007.

claim: Increased levels of glutamic acid and aspartic acid, both associated with the citric acid cycle, display a typical stress response consistent with the cold metabolomes of A. thaliana.
source: Likewise, increased levels of glutamic acid and aspartic acid, both associated with the citric acid cycle, display a typical stress response consistent with the cold metabolomes of A. thaliana (Kaplan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the metabolite data and a citation to Kaplan et al., 2004.

claim: DAPC illustrates a metabolomic response of all clusters to temperature stress (cold treatment at 5°C).
source: When grouping the data by temperature treatment, DAPC illustrates a metabolomic response of all clusters to temperature stress (cold treatment at 5°C; Figure 4d; Appendix 1—figure 30).
evidence: This is supported by the DAPC analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: No demarcation of the cold responses could be revealed either among the four bioclimatically defined groups of species and accessions of Cochlearia or even between Cochlearia and Ionopsidium.
source: Although our data set comprises different species from two genera spanning a large distribution range from the Mediterranean toward the Artic no demarcation of the cold responses could be revealed either among the four bioclimatically defined groups of species and accessions of Cochlearia or even between Cochlearia and Ionopsidium (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by the DAPC analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The putative high pleiotropy inherent in metabolism may force compensatory variants, which are then private in evolutionary lineages, species, or accessions.
source: The putative high pleiotropy inherent in metabolism may also force compensatory variants, which are then private in evolutionary lineages, species, or accessions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about metabolic evolution.

claim: Crossing experiments in A. thaliana accessions have shown that progenies have a much wider diversity of primary cold metabolism phenotypes, suggesting that when crossing the harmony of primary and compensatory mutations is broken.
source: Crossing experiments in A. thaliana accession have shown that progenies have a much wider diversity of primary cold metabolism phenotypes, which is suggesting that when crossing the harmony of primary and compensatory mutations is broken and then a wider distribution of phenotypes will emerge.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from A. thaliana studies.

claim: The concept of compensatory mutations may contribute to explain the evolutionary success of the putative hybrid and allopolyploid Cochlearia taxa, and point toward parallel evolution.
source: This concept may also contribute to explain the evolutionary success of the putative hybrid and allopolyploid Cochlearia taxa, and pointing toward parallel evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: Detailed knowledge on past and recent genetic admixture is essential to infer parallel evolution in polyploid Cochlearia taxa.
source: However, in particular with the polyploid Cochlearia taxa detailed knowledge on past and recent genetic admixture is essential to infer parallel evolution, and herein presented metabolomic data cannot contribute to shed light on parallel and adaptive evolution of Cochlearia polyploids.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the metabolomic data.

claim: Previous studies provided first insights into the complex evolutionary history of the genus Cochlearia.
source: Previous studies provided first insights into the complex evolutionary history of the genus Cochlearia (e.g., Koch et al., 1996; Koch et al., 1998; Koch et al., 1999; Koch, 2002; Koch et al., 2003; Kochjarová et al., 2006; Cieslak et al., 2007; Koch, 2012; Brandrud et al., 2017; Bray et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: A genus-wide picture of Cochlearia evolution has been missing.
source: Yet, a genus-wide picture has been missing.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Almost all Cochlearia taxa are declining since they strongly depend on the existence of cold habitats, which are among the first to be influenced by globally rising temperatures.
source: Today, living in a warming world, almost all of these taxa are declining since they strongly depend on the existence of cold habitats, which are among the first to be influenced by globally rising temperatures and the resultant transformations in abiotic conditions (Walther et al., 2002; Parmesan, 2006; Alsos et al., 2012; Barrett et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to climate change literature.

claim: There is an early split of two diploid gene pools followed by separation of the two diploid metapopulations in Arctic regions (2n=14) and in Europe (2n=12).
source: As revealed from the continental-scale geographical partitioning of diploid cytotypes (2n=12 and 2n=14; Figure 1a), we see an early split of two diploid gene pools followed by separation of the two diploid metapopulations in Arctic regions (2n=14) and in Europe (2n=12).
evidence: This is supported by cytogenetic and phylogenetic data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Only in Iceland do both diploid cytotypes (2n=12 and 2n=14) co-occur.
source: Only in Iceland do both diploid cytotypes co-occur.
evidence: This is supported by cytogenetic data.

claim: Both diploid cytotypes (2n=12 and 2n=14) underwent genome and chromosome size reduction within the Arctic environment.
source: Both cytotypes underwent genome and chromosome size reduction within this Arctic environment, which may be seen as a metabolic advantage (e.g., meiotic cell division under cold stress Bomblies et al., 2015, or triggered by shorter life cycles).
evidence: This is supported by cytogenetic data and a citation to Bomblies et al., 2015.

claim: Genome and chromosome size reduction may be seen as a metabolic advantage (e.g., meiotic cell division under cold stress or triggered by shorter life cycles).
source: Both cytotypes underwent genome and chromosome size reduction within this Arctic environment, which may be seen as a metabolic advantage (e.g., meiotic cell division under cold stress Bomblies et al., 2015, or triggered by shorter life cycles).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Bomblies et al., 2015.

claim: From a phylogenetic point of view, the most parsimonious scenario recognizes 2n=14 and thus a base chromosome number of n=7 as ancestral state.
source: As shown below from a phylogenetic point of view, the most parsimonious scenario recognizes 2n=14 and thus a base chromosome number of n=7 as ancestral state (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ancestral and exclusively circum-Arctic 2n=14 taxa may have benefitted from one extra centromere, which increases total recombination rate and thus may also be favorable under harsh conditions and drastic environmental changes.
source: A possible, but far from causal, hypothesis is that the ancestral and exclusively circum-Arctic 2n=14 taxa may have also benefitted from one extra centromere, which increases total recombination rate and thus may also be favorable under harsh conditions and drastic environmental changes (Stapley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation to Stapley et al., 2017.

claim: Aneuploidies in Cochlearia could be the result of hybridization/polyploidization events followed by mitotic/meiotic difficulties or independent ascending/descending dysploidies via chromosome rearrangements.
source: Whereas the presence of chromosomal aberrations in Cochlearia has been postulated to be caused by B-chromosomes (Gill, 1971b; Gill, 1973; Gill et al., 1978; Nordal, 1988), these aneuploidies could also be the result of hybridization/polyploidization events followed by mitotic/meiotic difficulties or independent ascending/descending dysploidies via chromosome rearrangements (Lysak, 2014), although the exact mechanisms in this genus are yet unclear.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Karyotypic variation and aneuploidy following hybridization in plants have been described as adjustment processes within the allopolyploid genome putatively connected to the beginning of re-diploidization.
source: Karyotypic variation and aneuploidy following hybridization in plants have been described as adjustment processes within the allopolyploid genome putatively connected to the beginning of re-diploidization (Mandáková et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mandáková et al., 2016.

claim: For Cochlearia, the high frequency of chromosomal aberrations in polyploids likely reflects a highly dynamic genome evolution, given the near absence of interspecific fertility barriers between cytotypes.
source: For Cochlearia, the high frequency of chromosomal aberrations in polyploids likely reflects a highly dynamic genome evolution, given the near absence of interspecific fertility barriers between cytotypes (Gill, 1971a; Gill, 1973; Koch et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: A trend for reducing genomic redundancy in the young polyploids is suggested by the negative correlation of chromosome size with increasing chromosome numbers.
source: Moreover, a trend for reducing genomic redundancy in the young polyploids is suggested by the negative correlation of chromosome size with increasing chromosome numbers.
evidence: This is an inference based on cytogenetic data.

claim: The patterns of genome dynamics in Cochlearia are well in accordance with the hypothesis of a necessary balance between both genomic flexibility and stability allowing for further adaptive evolution to a continuously changing environment.
source: Combined with the stable diploid karyotypes, these patterns are well in accordance with the hypothesis of a necessary balance between both genomic flexibility and stability allowing for further adaptive evolution to a continuously changing environment (Hohmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Hohmann et al., 2015.

claim: A tight concurrence of high glacial periods and diversification times within the six major lineages of Cochlearia was observed.
source: Despite the highly fluid genome dynamics across the genus, we did observe a tight concurrence of high glacial periods and diversification times within the six major lineages (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the BEAST analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The tight concurrence of high glacial periods and diversification times suggests a boosting impact of these climatic fluctuations on the diversification of the genus Cochlearia.
source: This suggests a boosting impact of these climatic fluctuations on the diversification of the genus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation.

claim: The observed polytomies, especially within the green and the purple lineage, likely reflect events of rapid, reticulate radiation during the last two glacial periods.
source: Accordingly, the observed polytomies, especially within the green and the purple lineage, likely reflect events of rapid, reticulate radiation during the last two glacial periods, where we speculate that polyploidization and hybridization may have facilitated adaptation to dramatically changing environments (Hohmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by a citation to Hohmann et al., 2015.

claim: Polyploidization and hybridization may have facilitated adaptation to dramatically changing environments in Cochlearia.
source: Accordingly, the observed polytomies, especially within the green and the purple lineage, likely reflect events of rapid, reticulate radiation during the last two glacial periods, where we speculate that polyploidization and hybridization may have facilitated adaptation to dramatically changing environments (Hohmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Hohmann et al., 2015.

claim: Based on the organellar phylogenies and divergence-time estimates, an evolutionary scenario with an ancestral base chromosome number of n=7 in diploid Arctic ancestors followed by reduction to n=6 in European diploids is most parsimonious.
source: Based on the organellar phylogenies and divergence-time estimates (and contradicting former hypotheses [Gill, 1971a; Gill, 1973; Koch et al., 1996]), an evolutionary scenario with an ancestral base chromosome number of n=7 in diploid Arctic ancestors followed by reduction to n=6 in European diploids is most parsimonious.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic and cytogenetic data.

claim: Additional glacial refugia must have existed in Europe north of the primary refugia for European species (Iberian Peninsula, Southern Italy, Balkans).
source: However, in accordance with former hypotheses (Koch, 2002; Koch et al., 2003), we can also postulate that additional glacial refugia must have existed in Europe north of the primary refugia for European species (Iberian Peninsula, Southern Italy, Balkans; Taberlet et al., 1998), as also described for other taxa (Stewart and Lister, 2001; Tribsch et al., 2002; Tribsch and Schönswetter, 2003; Provan and Bennett, 2008).
evidence: This is a postulate supported by citations.

claim: The putative Arctic background of the entire genus Cochlearia might have promoted the general association with cold-characterized habitat types throughout the genus.
source: The putative Arctic background of the entire genus Cochlearia might have (a) promoted the general association with cold-characterized habitat types throughout the genus and (b) facilitated later adaptation to different high alpine regions in Europe.
evidence: This is a speculative inference.

claim: The putative Arctic background of the entire genus Cochlearia might have facilitated later adaptation to different high alpine regions in Europe.
source: The putative Arctic background of the entire genus Cochlearia might have (a) promoted the general association with cold-characterized habitat types throughout the genus and (b) facilitated later adaptation to different high alpine regions in Europe.
evidence: This is a speculative inference.

claim: Adaptation to alpine habitats has taken place repeatedly in the High Tatra Mountains (C. tatrae), in the Austrian Alps (C. excelsa), in alpine habitat types in Great Britain (C. alpina/C. micacea), and in several other European habitats with a more subalpine character.
source: As revealed from the plastid phylogeny (Appendix 1—figure 6), the latter has taken place repeatedly in the High Tatra Mountains (C. tatrae, orange lineage, Eastern Europe), in the Austrian Alps (C. excelsa, green lineage, Arctic-European), in alpine habitat types in Great Britain (C. alpina/C. micacea, purple lineage, western European), and in several other European habitats with a more subalpine character, namely in the Pyrenees or in Switzerland.
evidence: This is supported by the plastid phylogeny shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: The very strong admixture between both diploid genetic clusters of different chromosome numbers (as seen in diploid Arctic Icelandic accessions) provides evidence of genetic coherence.
source: With respect to the putative Arctic origin of the genus in its current shape with an ancestral base chromosome number of n=7, the very strong admixture between both diploid genetic clusters of different chromosome numbers (as seen in diploid Arctic Icelandic accessions) provides evidence of genetic coherence.
evidence: This is supported by the STRUCTURE analysis.

claim: The two early separated gene pools serve as a continuous source for the evolution of new, often transient, and currently highly endangered species in Cochlearia.
source: Considering the numerous polyploids and their independent, multiple origins in Cochlearia (see Appendix 1) and the exceptional case of sympatry of both different diploid cytotypes in an arctic environment in Iceland, it seems that the two early separated gene pools serve as a continuous source for the evolution of new, often transient, and currently highly endangered species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic and phylogenetic data.

claim: ARC and EUR metapopulations are only weakly differentiated and share most of their genetic variation, either because of recent separation or gene flow.
source: Regarding the demographic histories of the two gene pools, our ABC data suggest that ARC and EUR metapopulations are only weakly differentiated and share most of their genetic variation, either because of recent separation or gene flow.
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results.

claim: ARC and EUR currently have large and similar effective population sizes, but ARC has expanded after a bottleneck whereas EUR has remained constant, or recently declined.
source: They currently have large and similar effective population sizes, but ARC has expanded after a bottleneck whereas EUR has remained constant, or recently declined.
evidence: This is supported by the ABC modeling results.

claim: When exposed to low but non-freezing temperatures, plants commonly activate cold acclimation responses involving changes in gene expression, enzymatic activities and ultimately, concentrations of many central carbon intermediates.
source: When exposed to low but non-freezing temperatures, plants commonly activate cold acclimation responses involving changes in gene expression, enzymatic activities and ultimately, concentrations of many central carbon intermediates (Kaplan et al., 2004; Kaplan et al., 2007; Hoermiller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to plant physiology literature.

claim: As part of the low temperature response, particular accumulations of carbohydrates, polyols, and amino acids are detected.
source: As part of this low temperature response, particular accumulations of carbohydrates, polyols, and amino acids are detected (Kaplan et al., 2004; Krasensky and Jonak, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to plant physiology literature.

claim: All Cochlearia and Ionopsidium species analyzed showed the cold acclimation response.
source: All Cochlearia and Ionopsidium species analyzed herein showed this response, too.
evidence: This is supported by the metabolite profiling data.

claim: Despite covering a broad phylogenetic and taxonomic diversity and clustering taxa according to bioclimatically defined clusters, low temperature response did not differentiate among those in Cochlearia.
source: However, despite covering a broad phylogenetic and taxonomic diversity and clustering taxa according to bioclimatically defined clusters, low temperature response did not differentiate among those, as it has been demonstrated for A. thaliana across a gradient from the Mediterranean toward Scandinavia (Weiszmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the metabolite profiling data and a citation to Weiszmann et al., 2020.

claim: The similar responses to cold within the genus Cochlearia reflect continuous connections to cold-characterized habitats acquired over the course of a migration to northern/circum-Arctic regions during the early evolution of the genus.
source: Given that all Cochlearia species, regardless of origin and habitat type, exhibited similar responses to the temperature treatment performed under controlled conditions for central carbon intermediates, we hypothesize that these similar responses to cold within the genus reflect continuous connections to cold-characterized habitats acquired over the course of a migration to northern/circum-Arctic regions during the early evolution of the genus.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the metabolite profiling data.

claim: A constitutive cold tolerance has not been lost secondarily within Cochlearia.
source: Apparently, a constitutive cold tolerance has not been lost secondarily within Cochlearia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolite profiling data.

claim: Previous studies on glucosinolate and tropane alkaloid chemotypes have shown rapid structural diversification and ecotype specificities within the Cochlearia genus.
source: In this respect, previous studies on glucosinolate and tropane alkaloid chemotypes, which are key to biotic stress adaptation, have shown rapid structural diversification and ecotype specificities within the Cochlearia genus (Brock et al., 2006; Blažević et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brock et al., 2006 and Blažević et al., 2020.

claim: Regarding the overall similar response of central carbon metabolism to the cold treatment of annual species from the genus Ionopsidium, commonalities between cold and salinity/drought stress would enable a putative recruitment of the cold tolerance from existing adaptations to drought and/or salt.
source: Regarding the overall similar response of central carbon metabolism to the cold treatment of annual species from the genus Ionopsidium, which are adapted to at least seasonally dry habitats and/or salt habitats, we may conclude that commonalities between cold and salinity/drought stress would enable a putative recruitment of the cold tolerance from existing adaptations to drought and/or salt as hypothesized for other plant taxa (Böndel et al., 2018; Exposito-Alonso et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion supported by citations to Böndel et al., 2018 and Exposito-Alonso et al., 2017.

claim: Both drought, salt and cold stress strongly involve osmotic challenge.
source: Because both drought, salt and cold stress strongly involve osmotic challenge, our data also support the idea that an evolution to one of these stressors in the common ancestor not only allowed for the survival under Mediterranean conditions (Ionopsidium), but also may have preadapted the nascent Cochlearia genus to habitats characterized by cold or salt, and with Arctic environments often characterized by drought, too.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about plant stress physiology.

claim: An evolution to one of these stressors (drought, salt, cold) in the common ancestor not only allowed for the survival under Mediterranean conditions (Ionopsidium), but also may have preadapted the nascent Cochlearia genus to habitats characterized by cold or salt.
